---
title: "data drift & concept drift"
---

## distinguish the signals

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| term | definition | example |
|---|---|---|
| data drift | a change in the input distribution, $p(x)$ | a different mix of input feature values |
| prediction drift | a change in the model’s output distribution | more high predicted probabilities |
| target distribution change | a change in observed outcome frequencies, $p(y)$ | a positive class becomes more common |
| concept drift | a change in the outcome relationship conditional on inputs, $p(y\mid x)$ | the same inputs become associated with different outcomes |

:::

- these signals can occur together; input drift alone does not establish concept drift or a loss of predictive quality [drift definitions](https://www.evidentlyai.com/ml-in-production/concept-drift)
- investigate schema, units, feature-generation code, reference files, and label definitions before deciding that the underlying process changed

## compare a reference and a current window

- a reference is a versioned baseline distribution; the current window contains the newer observations being compared
- compare compatible populations and periods, accounting for seasonality and repeated entities
- check missingness and invalid values separately rather than hiding them inside a distribution test
- scipy is a scientific-computing library; its two-sample kolmogorov–smirnov test compares numeric sample distributions
- the ks statistic is the largest gap between empirical cumulative distributions, the fractions of observations at or below each value [ks documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.ks_2samp.html)

```python
reference = pd.read_csv("monitoring-output/reference.csv")["feature"]
current = pd.read_csv("monitoring-output/current.csv")["feature"]
result = ks_2samp(reference.dropna(), current.dropna())
print({"ks_statistic": float(result.statistic), "pvalue": float(result.pvalue),
       "current_missing_fraction": float(current.isna().mean())})
```

- import pandas as `pd` and `ks_2samp` from `scipy.stats`; the [download](../../examples/monitoring-demo.zip) includes a checked helper in `drift_metrics.py`
- a p-value describes how surprising the statistic is under the null hypothesis that the two distributions are the same, assuming the test’s conditions hold; it is not the probability that the model is failing
- a small p-value can accompany a tiny change in a large sample; inspect the statistic, feature meaning, and downstream impact too
- ks p-values assume independent samples from continuous distributions; tied counts, categorical data, and dependent observations need an appropriate method or calibration
- testing many features increases false-alert risk; account for multiple comparisons rather than treating every p-value independently, and require practical impact before escalation

## turn a flag into an investigation

- evidently is a library for data/model evaluation and monitoring reports; use it when many features and quality checks need a common reporting workflow [metric catalogue](https://docs.evidentlyai.com/metrics/all_metrics)
- the exercise flags a ks statistic above 0.15 for review and reports missingness separately; this is a toy effect threshold, not a universal drift rule
- identify affected features and groups, inspect pipeline changes, and compare model quality when labels mature
- a drift flag can lead to a pipeline fix, more investigation, or retraining; it does not automatically approve a replacement

## log results so trends are visible over time

- a single drift check answers "is this batch different from the reference"; logging every batch's results to the same place turns that into a trend you can see change gradually, not just a one-off alert
- mlflow isn't only for training runs — the same [tracking api](../experiments/tracking.qmd) can log a monitoring or qc check as its own run, with the batch/window identifier as a tag so related checks can be queried together

```python
import mlflow

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///mlflow.db")
mlflow.set_experiment("drift-monitoring")
with mlflow.start_run(run_name=f"batch-{batch_id}"):
    mlflow.set_tags({"batch_id": batch_id, "reference_version": reference_version})
    mlflow.log_metrics({
        "ks_statistic": float(result.statistic),
        "ks_pvalue": float(result.pvalue),
        "missing_fraction": float(current.isna().mean()),
    })
```

- querying this experiment's runs over time — through the mlflow ui or `mlflow.search_runs` — gives the trend line a single alert can't: whether a statistic is drifting gradually, jumped once, or oscillates with a known cycle
- keep this separate from the training-run experiment used in [experiment tracking](../experiments/tracking.qmd); mixing monitoring checks into the same experiment as training runs makes both harder to query
- the same pattern logs any recurring quality check, not just drift — a per-batch or per-run qc summary belongs here as readily as a ks statistic, as long as it's logged with a consistent tag so later runs are comparable
